004.t: Characters, ASCII, Unicode and Data Units
o: Explain how text is represented using character codes.
Convert simple quantities of bits and bytes.
r: Convert hexadecimal 0F to denary.
What does the nibble 1010 represent in hexadecimal?
A.
What happens when the 8-bit number 00010010 is shifted left one place?
A program adds 11110000 and 00010000. Explain the unsigned 8-bit overflow and give the true denary sum.
240 + 16 = 256, which is beyond the 0–255 range; requires 9 bits.
c: Characters need codes
Computers store character codes as binary. A character set maps each character to its numerical representation.
ASCII and Unicode
Standard ASCII provides a small character set; Unicode supports characters from many more languages and writing systems.
Bits to bytes
A bit stores 0 or 1; 4 bits form a nibble, 8 form a byte. Convert bits to bytes by dividing by eight.
Encoding affects size
Text storage depends on the number of characters and the number of bits or bytes used by the particular encoding. Do not assume every Unicode character uses one byte.

m.q: A text message contains 12 characters, each encoded using exactly 8 bits. Find its raw size in bytes and explain the character-code assumption.
st: Identify the given encoding: 8 bits per character (one byte).
Multiply 12 characters × 8 bits = 96 bits.
Convert bits to bytes: 96 ÷ 8 = 12 bytes.
State that headers and metadata are excluded; Unicode encoding can use different byte lengths.

w: A text label has 18 characters, each stored using 8 bits. Calculate bits.
Convert 144 bits into bytes.
Why can Unicode be more useful than ASCII for a multilingual school website?
Unicode can represent letters and symbols from far more languages than standard ASCII.

k.q: Predict what a program prints when it stores a numerical character code.
p: Explain why printing 66 is not the same as printing the character B.
k.a: It prints 65, then 66 after the change. The stored number is printed as a number; converting it into a character requires a character-conversion operation. Standard ASCII capital A and B have codes 65 and 66; memorising them is not required.

e: State the number of bits in a byte and a nibble. [2 marks]
Byte: 8 bits [1]; nibble: 4 bits [1].
Explain one advantage of Unicode over ASCII. [2 marks]
Unicode has a much larger repertoire of characters [1], allowing many different languages and writing systems [1].
A file has 80 characters, each taking 16 bits under a given encoding. Calculate raw data size in bytes. [3 marks]
v: A defined mapping from characters to numerical codes.
A relatively small character set used to represent text.
A standard supporting a very wide range of characters and symbols.
x: Every Unicode character must always be stored in exactly one byte.

005.t: Images, Pixels, Colour Depth and File Sizes
o: Explain pixels, resolution and colour depth.
Calculate an uncompressed bitmap's raw pixel-data size.
Convert a result from bits to bytes.
r: Name the character encoding standard that covers many writing systems.
Unicode.
Convert 48 bits into bytes.
6 bytes.
Convert binary 00010101 to denary.
A text file has 150 characters at 8 bits each. Calculate its raw size in bits and bytes.
1,200 bits = 150 bytes.
c: Bitmap images
A bitmap is made of pixels. Resolution describes its width and height in pixels.
Colour depth
Colour depth is bits allocated to each pixel. An n-bit colour depth can represent up to 2^n different colours.
Raw file-size method
Multiply width × height × colour depth to obtain bits. Divide by 8 to convert to bytes.
Assumptions
This calculates uncompressed pixel data only. File headers, metadata and compression may change the actual file size.

m.q: Calculate raw storage for an 8 × 8 bitmap at 2-bit colour depth.
st: Resolution is 8 × 8 = 64 pixels.
Each pixel uses 2 bits, so 64 × 2 = 128 bits.
Convert to bytes: 128 ÷ 8 = 16 bytes.
State the unit and the assumption: no headers or compression.

w: A bitmap is 10 × 6 pixels. How many pixels are there?
60 pixels.
At 4-bit colour depth, how many bits for that image?
Convert the 240 bits to bytes and explain what happens if depth doubles.
240 ÷ 8 = 30 bytes; doubling depth doubles raw pixel-data size to 60 bytes.

k.q: Predict the raw image pixel-data size calculated in bits.
k.code:
width = 10
height = 8
depth = 4
print(width * height * depth)
p: Change depth to 8 and predict again.
Write one extra print expression for bytes.
k.a: 10 × 8 × 4 = 320 bits. At 8-bit depth: 640 bits. A second print may be print(width * height * depth / 8) to display 80 bytes at depth 8.

e: State what is meant by a pixel and colour depth. [2 marks]
Pixel: smallest individual element in a bitmap [1]; colour depth: bits used to represent each pixel's colour [1].
A bitmap is 12 × 5 pixels at 4-bit colour depth. Calculate raw bits and bytes. [3 marks]
A 1,000 × 800 bitmap has 8-bit colour depth. Calculate raw storage in MB using 1,000 bytes per KB and 1,000 KB per MB. [4 marks]
v: One individual picture element of a bitmap.
The number of pixels across and down an image.
Bits used to store a pixel's colour.
Additional information stored about a file or image.
x: Doubling colour depth doubles the uncompressed pixel-data size if dimensions stay the same.

006.t: Sound, Sampling, Bit Depth and File Sizes
o: Explain how analogue sound is sampled for digital storage.
Distinguish sample rate from bit depth.
Calculate raw uncompressed mono sound data size.
r: Define colour depth.
Number of bits used to represent one bitmap pixel.
A 5 × 4 image at 8 bits per pixel takes how many raw bytes?
5 × 4 × 8 = 160 bits = 20 bytes.
Why does Unicode matter for international text?
It supports a much wider range of characters than ASCII.
An 8 × 8 image at 2-bit colour depth becomes 8-bit. Calculate how many more raw bytes it needs.
Original 16 bytes; new 64 bytes; increase of 48 bytes.
c: Analogue versus digital
Real sound is continuous. To digitise it, a computer samples the wave at regular intervals and stores measurements as binary.
Sample rate
Sample rate is the number of samples measured per second, in hertz (Hz). More samples can capture more detail.
Bit depth
Bit depth is the number of bits available for each sample's amplitude; more bits allow finer amplitude representation.
Raw mono sound
Raw bits = sample rate × seconds × bit depth. Divide by eight for bytes. Channels, headers and compression can change real file size.

m.q: A mono clip uses 10 samples per second, lasts 5 seconds and uses 8 bits per sample. Find the raw size.
st: Write the formula: rate × duration × bit depth.
10 samples/s × 5 seconds = 50 samples.
400 ÷ 8 = 50 bytes (raw, mono, uncompressed).

w: A sound clip has sample rate 20 Hz and duration 10 s. How many samples?
20 × 10 = 200 samples.
The clip uses 8 bits per sample. How many raw bits?
Calculate bytes and state how the size changes if duration doubles.
1,600 ÷ 8 = 200 bytes; doubling duration doubles the data size to 400 bytes.

k.q: Predict the number of raw sound bits from three variables.
k.code:
rate = 20
seconds = 4
depth = 8
print(rate * seconds * depth)
p: Write one print statement to convert bits into bytes.
k.a: 20 × 4 × 8 = 640 bits. For 5 seconds: 800 bits. print(rate * seconds * depth / 8) gives 100 bytes for the revised duration.

e: State what is meant by sample rate. [2 marks]
The number of sound samples taken [1] every second [1].
Explain how increasing bit depth affects sound quality and raw file size. [3 marks]
More bits represent each sample [1], allowing more accurate representation of amplitude [1], but increasing raw file size [1].
A mono recording is sampled at 1,000 Hz for 4 seconds, using 8 bits per sample. Calculate its raw size in bytes. [3 marks]
v: Number of samples taken per second.
Number of bits representing each sample.
Length of the sound recording in seconds.
x: Doubling sample rate doubles uncompressed mono sound data size when all other values stay fixed.

o: Calculate storage saved and convert between units.
r: What does sound bit depth measure?
Bits used to represent each digital sound sample's amplitude.
Convert 3,200 bits to bytes.
400 bytes.
What is colour depth?
Bits used for each pixel.
A mono clip is recorded at 100 samples/s for 5 seconds at 8 bits/sample. Calculate its raw size in bytes.
c: Why compress files?
Compression reduces the amount of storage needed and can reduce transmission times.
Lossless
Lossless compression makes files smaller while allowing exact reconstruction of every original bit. Use it for source code and important documents.
Lossy
Lossy compression permanently removes some data. It can reduce photos, music or video file sizes when some loss of quality is acceptable.
Calculating savings
Storage saved = original size − compressed size. Keep units consistent; if asked for a percentage, divide by original size and multiply by 100.

m.q: A text program and a photograph must be compressed. Choose a method for each and calculate the saving if a photo falls from 800 KB to 500 KB.
st: Source code must remain exact, so choose lossless compression.
A website photograph may use lossy compression if some detail loss is acceptable.
Subtract compressed size: 800 KB − 500 KB = 300 KB saved.
Percentage saved = 300 ÷ 800 × 100 = 37.5%.

w: Should a spreadsheet containing exact examination marks use lossy or lossless compression? Explain.
Lossless: all original data must be recoverable exactly.
A 900 KB image compresses to 600 KB. How many KB were saved?
What percentage of the original file size was saved?

k.q: Predict how much file space is saved by compression.
p: Explain why this program does not itself compress a file.
k.a: It prints 300 KB, then 400 KB after the change. This is a calculation of the saving only, not a compression algorithm.

e: Identify one reason to compress a file. [1 mark]
It requires less storage or may transfer faster [1].
Explain why lossless compression is appropriate for computer program files. [2 marks]
The original file must be recovered exactly [1], because losing any original instructions could corrupt the program [1].
A sound file falls from 12 MB to 9 MB after compression. Calculate storage saved and justify whether lossy may be suitable for online listening. [4 marks]
12 − 9 = 3 MB saved [1]. Lossy may be suitable [1] because some sound information can be discarded to reduce file size [1], provided quality remains acceptable for the purpose [1].
v: Reducing the number of bits needed to represent a file.
Compression that allows the original to be restored exactly.
Compression that permanently removes some original data.
The quantity of storage required for a file.
x: Lossless compression can reproduce the exact original data.

008.t: Primary Storage: RAM, ROM and Cache
o: Explain the jobs of RAM, ROM and cache.
Apply memory concepts to a familiar computer.
r: Explain one difference between lossy and lossless compression.
Lossless can restore the original exactly; lossy permanently removes some detail.
Why does an 8-bit image require more raw space than a 2-bit image of the same resolution?
Each pixel stores more bits (four times as many).
Convert 80 bits to bytes.
10 bytes.
A document must be identical after decompression but a website thumbnail may be slightly lower quality. Choose a compression type for each and justify.
Document: lossless, exact restoration. Thumbnail: lossy may be acceptable to reduce transfer and storage costs.
c: Why is memory needed?
Running programs need fast access to instructions and working data. Primary storage supports the CPU while programs run.
RAM
Random Access Memory stores programs and data currently in use. It is volatile, so its contents are lost when power is removed.
ROM
Read Only Memory is non-volatile and commonly stores firmware or start-up instructions.
Cache
CPU cache is small, very fast memory close to the processor holding frequently used data and instructions, reducing access time.

m.q: A laptop starts, opens a game, saves a level, then powers off. Explain what each type of memory does.
st: Non-volatile ROM/firmware supplies start-up instructions.
The active operating system and game data are loaded into RAM from secondary storage.
The processor can access frequently needed data faster from cache.
Saving writes the level to non-volatile secondary storage; RAM contents are lost at power-off.

w: A word processor is open. Where is its working data held?
RAM.
Where might the instructions needed to start a device be stored?
ROM or another form of non-volatile firmware storage.
Why does the CPU use cache even though the computer has RAM?
Cache is much faster and can hold frequently needed instructions/data, reducing time accessing RAM.

k.q: Predict how a working variable changes during program execution.
p: Explain why this is a model of changing working data, not a simulation of ROM.
k.a: It prints 15, or 20 after the change. Variables illustrate data that changes while a program runs; this is not physical memory hardware.

e: State one difference between RAM and ROM. [2 marks]
RAM is volatile [1], while ROM is non-volatile [1].
Explain the purpose of cache memory. [2 marks]
Holds frequently used instructions or data near the CPU [1], enabling faster access than repeatedly fetching from RAM [1].
A pupil saves a document, switches off the laptop and turns it on again. Explain why the document remains but unsaved work could be lost. [4 marks]

Saved file persists on non-volatile secondary storage [1]. RAM is volatile [1] and holds working data while the laptop operates [1]. Unsaved edits may be lost when RAM contents disappear at power-off [1].
v: Volatile working memory for programs and data in use.
Small, very fast memory used by the CPU.
Loses stored contents when power is removed.
x: RAM usually retains its contents when the power is off.
